The study uses a combination of physical and computational experiments.
The flow conditions studied are subsonic and moderately transonic turbine flows.
The film cooling scheme used is a showerhead film cooling arrangement with five staggered rows of holes.
The pitch-to-diameter ratio of the film holes is 4.0.
The angle of the film holes to the blade surface is 30 degrees in the spanwise direction and 90 degrees in the streamwise direction.
The steady computation is used to isolate the time-average effect of wake passing on film cooling performance.
The maximum time step used in the unsteady calculation is limited by grid spacing at the wall.
The number of grid points used in the blade-to-blade direction is 305 points tangential to the blade and 90 points normal to the blade.
The maximum CFL number used in the unsteady calculation is about 7.7.
The difference in film effectiveness between the unsteady and steady solutions is up to 8 percent.
Wake passing can cause the coolant flow to be turned more in the chordwise direction on the suction side and more in the spanwise direction on the pressure side.
The staggered hole arrangement can cause flow from adjacent rows to merge, resulting in the appearance of discrete jets at the surface.
Time-average particle traces are used to visualize the flow from the film holes.
The study uses a rotating rod arrangement to produce a periodic wake pattern.
The NASALewis Rotor-Wake Heat Transfer Rig is used as an experimental facility.
The study uses a three-dimensional viscous turbulent calculation to model the flow field.
The Baldwin-Lomax turbulence model is used in the calculation.
The code RVC3D is used to solve the thin-layer Navier-Stokes equations.
The study uses a C-grid with implicit residual smoothing.
The maximum number of wake passings required for the solution to converge is 13.
